title: DMS to Decimal Converter: For GIS and Maps
description: Convert degrees-minutes-seconds coordinates to decimal degrees with DMS to Decimal — paste DMS, get GIS-ready decimals. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, 40°45′28.8″N, 73°59′07.8″W pastes in from a chart and comes out as 40.7580, −73.9855 — ready for every map and database on earth.
quick_answer: DMS to Decimal converts degrees-minutes-seconds coordinates into decimal degrees for GIS and web maps. Paste the DMS pair and read the signed decimals — hemispheres folded into signs, minutes and seconds divided by 60 and 3,600, all the carries handled by the converter instead of your patience.

A form gave you DMS fields and your source gave decimals — or the reverse. Convert the source once; never retype a digit.
40°45′28.8″ = 40 + 45/60 + 28.8/3600 = 40 + 0.75 + 0.008 = 40.7580°. The longitude: 73 + 59/60 + 7.8/3600 = 73.9855, signed negative for W. Two divisions and a sign — easy to say, tedious at scale.
Seconds written as 60 or more in a source (40°45′60″) signal a rounding artefact upstream. The converter normalises the arithmetic; the value's provenance is your eyebrow's job.

faq: Can it handle mixed formats?
DMS pairs in the common dresses (symbols, spaces, letters) parse here; truly mangled strings go through the Coordinate Parser first, which is built for mess.
Which datum do these coordinate tools use?
WGS84 assumed — conversion changes dress, not datum. A DMS pair from an old-datum chart converts faithfully and lands offset; that is a datum question, and it is flagged rather than hidden.
Do more decimal places always mean better accuracy?
Output decimals are arithmetic: 28.8″ of input earns about 5 decimals of honest output (0.1″ ≈ 3 m). More places are costume.
Can I copy the result into GIS software?
Yes — signed decimals are GIS's native input, which is the entire purpose of the exercise.
Hemisphere letters or leading signs?
Both read correctly; letters set the sign, and a minus with a W would double-negate — the parser family flags the contradiction.
Seconds as decimals?
28.8″ style is native here — fractional seconds are the modern chart norm.
Batch conversion?
Pairs one at a time; columns belong to GIS imports, spot-checked against this page's arithmetic.
Degrees-minutes (no seconds)?
That is DDM — the Coordinate Converter dresses pairs that way; the division is minutes/60 alone.
It rejected my string.
Check order (lat first), ranges (minutes and seconds under 60 in honest data) and symbols — the failure points at the component that broke.
Why does GIS hate DMS?
Because text formats invite a thousand parsers' disagreements; numbers invite none. Decimals are the interchange; DMS is the literature.
Antarctic and polar pairs?
Latitude to ±90 converts mechanically; longitude at the pole is a formality the arithmetic indulges.
